definition: Yellowing of leaves due to insufficient chlorophyll production, often caused by disease, nutrient deficiency, or environmental stress.
Death of plant tissue, appearing as brown or black dead areas on leaves, stems, or fruit.
A localized area of diseased or damaged plant tissue, often discolored and irregularly shaped.
A pattern of light and dark green or yellow patches on leaves caused by viral infections.
An organism (typically insect) that transmits a pathogen from infected to healthy plants.
Pathogen material (spores, bacteria, virus particles) capable of causing infection in a susceptible host.
A fungicide or insecticide that is absorbed and transported throughout the plant, providing internal protection.
A fungicide that remains on the plant surface and protects against infection but does not enter plant tissue.
The removal and destruction of infected plants to prevent the spread of disease to healthy plants.
Disease management practices that modify the growing environment, such as crop rotation, sanitation, and irrigation management.
Use of natural enemies (predators, parasites, pathogens) to control pests and diseases.
A chemical compound used to control fungal diseases.
A chemical compound used to control insect pests.
The reproductive structure of a fungus that produces and releases spores.
The vegetative part of a fungus, consisting of a network of fine white filaments (hyphae).
Premature dropping of leaves from a plant, often caused by disease, pest attack, or environmental stress.
Rapid and widespread killing of plant tissue, often causing leaves to brown and die quickly as if scorched by fire.
Abnormal plant growth or swelling caused by insects, nematodes, bacteria, or fungi, commonly found on roots or stems.
A compact mass of hardened fungal mycelium that can survive adverse conditions and germinate to produce new infection.
A single thread-like filament that makes up the vegetative body of a fungus.
Yellowing between leaf veins while veins remain green, typically indicating nutrient deficiency such as iron or magnesium.
A geographic area defined by similar climate, soil, and growing conditions that determine suitable crop production systems.
Growing two or more crops simultaneously on the same field to maximize land use and reduce pest pressure.
The practice of planting different crops sequentially on the same field to improve soil health and break pest and disease cycles.
Covering soil around plants with organic material (straw, leaves) or plastic to conserve moisture, suppress weeds, and regulate temperature.
A pest management system using repellent intercrops (push) and attractive trap crops (pull) to protect main crop from pests.
Application of fungicide, insecticide, or biological agents to seeds before planting to protect seedlings from early-season pests and diseases.
A chemical or biological agent used to control plant-parasitic nematodes in soil.
A pest control product derived from plants, such as neem oil, pyrethrum, or chili pepper extracts.
A biological product containing beneficial microorganisms (Trichoderma, Bacillus) used to control fungal plant diseases.
An airtight storage method that deprives grain pests of oxygen, effectively controlling storage insects without chemicals.
A soil disinfection method using clear plastic tarp to trap solar heat, killing soil-borne pathogens, weed seeds, and nematodes.
A symptom in cereals where the central growing point dies, causing the innermost leaf to brown and dry, often caused by stem borers.
A symptom in rice where panicles emerge empty, bleached, and unfilled due to stem borer damage cutting off nutrient flow.
A black fungal growth developing on honeydew excreted by sap-sucking insects like aphids, whiteflies, and mealybugs.
A sticky, sugary substance excreted by sap-feeding insects such as aphids, whiteflies, and scale insects.
Regular field inspection to monitor pest and disease levels and make timely management decisions.
A plant grown near the main crop to attract pests away, reducing damage to the primary crop.
Targeted application of fertilizer or pesticide only to areas that need treatment rather than whole-field broadcasting.
A locally adapted, traditional variety of a crop that has been developed over time through natural and farmer selection.
A technique for producing disease-free plantlets by growing plant cells in sterile laboratory conditions.
